decks.title: Evolution: Origin of Life and Evidences — Part 1: Origin of life and morphological evidence
goals: Explain the Oparin–Haldane theory and why a reducing atmosphere was needed
Distinguish protobionts and coacervates, and describe the Miller–Urey experiment
Distinguish homologous, analogous and vestigial organs with examples

slides.heading: Origin of life and evidences of evolution
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how life may have begun on Earth, and what the bodies of living organisms tell us about their common ancestry.

visual.alt: Flow of chemical evolution from simple gases to organic molecules to protobionts to the first cells

slides.narration: The Earth formed about four and a half billion years ago. Life probably appeared within a billion years, first as simple molecules built from the gases of the early atmosphere, then as droplets that could hold them together, and finally as the first cells.

slides.heading: Three old ideas about the origin of life
slides.body_md: Early explanations differed on whether life can arise from non-living matter.

rows: Life arises from non-living matter, such as maggots from rotting meat
Disproved for present conditions by Louis Pasteur’s swan-neck flask experiment
Life arises only from pre-existing life
Spores or units of life came to Earth from outer space
Does not explain how life began in the first place

visual.alt: Table comparing abiogenesis, biogenesis and panspermia

slides.narration: Pasteur boiled broth in flasks with long curved necks. Dust and microbes were trapped in the bend, and no life appeared, while broth in a broken flask soon teemed with microbes. So life today comes only from life. Yet the very first life must have arisen from non-living matter.

slides.heading: The Oparin–Haldane theory
slides.body_md: **A. I. Oparin (1924)** and **J. B. S. Haldane (1929)** proposed that life arose by **chemical evolution** in the early Earth’s **reducing atmosphere** of **methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour**, with **no free oxygen**. Energy from **lightning, UV radiation and volcanic heat** formed simple organic molecules, which collected in the sea as a **“hot dilute soup”**.

rows: Organic molecules formed were not oxidised or broken down
Strong UV radiation reached the surface as an energy source

visual.alt: Table of the conditions of the early Earth and why they mattered

slides.narration: Free oxygen is very reactive and would have destroyed the first organic molecules as fast as they formed. In an atmosphere without oxygen, sugars, amino acids and bases could build up in the oceans and react to form larger molecules.

slides.heading: Protobionts and coacervates
slides.body_md: **Protobionts** are aggregates of abiotically produced organic molecules, surrounded by a membrane-like layer, that keep an internal environment different from their surroundings. **Coacervates** (Oparin) are one kind: colloidal droplets of proteins and polysaccharides in water. **Microspheres** (Sidney Fox) are protein-like droplets formed by heating amino acids and cooling them in water.

rows: Any precursor of cells made abiotically
Colloidal droplets of proteins, polysaccharides and water
Not truly; some grow and divide
No; they can absorb substances and divide

visual.alt: Table distinguishing protobionts from coacervates

slides.narration: Neither coacervates nor microspheres are alive, but they show how a boundary could form around chemicals, keep them together, and allow simple reactions inside. That is an important step towards a cell.

slides.heading: The Miller–Urey experiment
slides.body_md: In **1953**, **Stanley Miller** and **Harold Urey** sealed **methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour** in a glass apparatus, passed **electric sparks** through the gases and boiled and condensed the water for about a **week**. The liquid in the trap contained **amino acids** such as glycine and alanine.

slides.narration: The sparks stood for lightning and the boiling water for the warm ocean. In about a week, simple amino acids formed from the gases alone. Later experiments also produced sugars, nitrogen bases, pigments and fats in similar conditions.

slides.body_md: Which statement about coacervates is correct?
slides.narration: Quick check. Are coacervates living cells, or droplets of colloids?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reasoning about the Miller–Urey set-up
slides.body_md: For each part of the apparatus, say what early-Earth condition it represented and what would happen if it were changed.
bullets: Conclusion: **organic molecules of life can form abiotically** from simple gases with an energy source.

rows: With oxygen added, few organic molecules survive
Without energy, no amino acids form
Gases and products would not circulate

visual.alt: Worked table relating each part of the Miller–Urey apparatus to early-Earth conditions

slides.narration: Each part of the apparatus matches a feature of the early Earth. Taking away the energy source, or adding oxygen, would stop amino acids from building up. That is why the result supports the Oparin and Haldane idea of chemical evolution.

slides.heading: Quick check: reducing atmosphere
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about the early atmosphere.
slides.narration: Quick check. What would free oxygen do to organic molecules?

slides.heading: Homologous organs and divergent evolution
slides.body_md: **Homologous organs** have the **same basic structure and origin** but may do **different jobs**. The forelimbs of a **human, cheetah, whale and bat** all have the humerus, radius and ulna, carpals, metacarpals and phalanges. In plants, the **thorn of Bougainvillea** and the **tendril of Cucurbita** are both modified stems. They show **divergent evolution** from a common ancestor.

slides.narration: The same set of bones has been stretched, shortened or fused to suit grasping, running, swimming or flying. Such a shared plan is best explained by descent from a common ancestor, followed by adaptation to different ways of life.

slides.heading: Analogous organs and convergent evolution
slides.body_md: **Analogous organs** do the **same job** but have **different structure and origin**. They arise by **convergent evolution**, when unrelated organisms adapt to similar needs.

rows: Wings of a butterfly and a bird
Eye of an octopus and a mammal
Flippers of a penguin and a dolphin

visual.alt: Table of analogous organ pairs

slides.narration: Similar problems, such as flying through air or storing food underground, often produce similar solutions in unrelated organisms. Analogous organs show that the environment shapes form, but they do not show close common ancestry.

slides.heading: Vestigial organs
slides.body_md: **Vestigial organs** are reduced, functionless (or nearly so) remnants of organs that were useful in ancestors.

rows: Birds and reptiles, as a third eyelid
Many mammals, to move the ears

visual.alt: Table of vestigial organs in humans

slides.narration: Why would a body keep parts that do nothing useful? Because they are inherited from ancestors in which they worked. Vestigial organs are therefore strong evidence of common descent.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: homologous or analogous?
slides.body_md: Classify each pair and name the kind of evolution it shows.
bullets: Ask: **same origin?** → homologous; **same function only?** → analogous.

rows: Forelimb of a whale and wing of a bat
Wing of an insect and wing of a bird
Thorn of Bougainvillea and tendril of Cucurbita

visual.alt: Worked table classifying organ pairs as homologous or analogous

slides.narration: Always ask about origin first. If two organs are built on the same plan and develop from the same part, they are homologous, whatever they now do. If they only share a function, they are analogous.

slides.heading: Quick check: analogous organs
slides.body_md: Which pair are analogous organs?
slides.narration: Quick check. Look for the same job but a different origin.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Abiogenesis (disproved for today by Pasteur), biogenesis, panspermia.
Oparin–Haldane: chemical evolution in a reducing atmosphere (methane, ammonia, hydrogen, water vapour; no free oxygen).
Protobionts: coacervates (Oparin), microspheres (Fox).
Miller–Urey (1953): sparks in reducing gases gave amino acids.
Homologous (same origin, divergent), analogous (same function, convergent), vestigial (reduced remnants).

rows: Descent from ancestors where they worked

visual.alt: Summary table of morphological evidences

slides.narration: To recap: life most likely began by chemical evolution in an atmosphere without oxygen, as the Miller and Urey experiment supports. The structure of living organisms, with homologous, analogous and vestigial organs, records how they have evolved.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Explain **why** a reducing atmosphere was needed.
Distinguish **protobionts** and **coacervates** precisely.
Give **two plant and two animal examples** each of homologous and analogous organs.
Label the **Miller–Urey** apparatus: gases, electrodes, condenser, trap.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Give the reason a reducing atmosphere mattered. Keep protobionts and coacervates apart. Learn two plant and two animal examples for each kind of organ. And be ready to label the Miller and Urey apparatus.

decks.title: Evolution: Origin of Life and Evidences — Part 2: Embryology, fossils, biogeography and molecules
goals: Explain the embryological evidence and the idea of recapitulation
Explain how fossils are dated by radiocarbon dating and relate eras to their dominant life
Use biogeographical and molecular evidence, and explain adaptive radiation

slides.heading: More lines of evidence
slides.body_md: Part 2 — evidence from embryos, fossils, the distribution of organisms and their molecules.

visual.alt: Flow of four further lines of evidence for evolution

slides.narration: Several independent kinds of evidence all point to the same conclusion: living organisms share common ancestors and have changed over time. We look at embryos, fossils, where organisms live, and the molecules inside them.

slides.heading: Embryological evidence
slides.body_md: Embryos of fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals look alike in early stages: all have **gill slits (pharyngeal pouches)**, a **notochord** and a **tail**. **Ernst Haeckel** proposed the **recapitulation theory**: **ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny** — development of an individual repeats the evolutionary history of its group.

rows: Gill slits in a human embryo
Embryos resemble embryos, not adults, of other groups (von Baer)
Recapitulation is not literal; it shows common descent

visual.alt: Table of embryological observations and interpretations

slides.narration: A human embryo never breathes through gills, but for a short time it has the same pouches that become gills in a fish. Karl Ernst von Baer showed that embryos resemble the embryos of other animals, not their adults, so the theory is not taken literally today.

slides.heading: Fossils and how they form
slides.body_md: **Fossils** are remains or traces of organisms preserved in rocks. Older rock layers (**strata**) lie deeper and hold simpler forms. **Archaeopteryx**, with feathers and wings like a bird but teeth, claws and a long bony tail like a reptile, is a **connecting link** between reptiles and birds.

rows: Bones and wood replaced by minerals
Insects in amber, mammoths in ice

visual.alt: Table of kinds of fossils

slides.narration: The fossil record shows a sequence: simple life in the oldest rocks, then fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals in younger layers. Connecting links like Archaeopteryx show features of two groups, just as evolution predicts.

slides.heading: Radiocarbon dating
slides.body_md: Living organisms take in carbon, including a constant small fraction of radioactive **carbon-14**. After death, no new carbon enters and carbon-14 decays with a **half-life of 5730 years**. Comparing the carbon-14 left with that in living tissue gives the **age**; the method works for remains up to about **50 000 years** old. Older rocks are dated with other isotopes, such as **uranium–lead**.

slides.narration: Each half-life, half of the remaining carbon fourteen decays. After one half-life a half is left, after two a quarter, after three an eighth. Measuring how much remains therefore tells us how long ago the organism died.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: dating a bone
slides.body_md: A bone contains one quarter of the carbon-14 found in living bone. How old is it? What fraction would be left after three half-lives?
bullets: $\dfrac{1}{4} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2}$, so 2 half-lives have passed.
Age $= 2 \times 5730 = 11460$ years.
After 3 half-lives: $\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{3} = 0.125$ of the original.

visual.alt: Worked table: one quarter left means 11460 years

slides.narration: One quarter is one half of one half, so two half-lives have passed. Two times five thousand seven hundred and thirty years is eleven thousand four hundred and sixty years. After a third half-life only an eighth would remain.

slides.heading: The geological time scale
slides.body_md: Earth’s history is divided into **eras**, each with its typical life (dates approximate, in million years ago).

rows: Age of mammals; flowering plants dominant; humans in the latest period
Age of reptiles (dinosaurs); gymnosperms dominant; first birds, mammals and flowering plants
Invertebrates, then fishes and amphibians; ferns and seed ferns form coal forests

visual.alt: Table of geological eras and their dominant flora and fauna

slides.narration: Each era is named for its life. The Palaeozoic, meaning ancient life, saw fishes and amphibians and great fern forests. The Mesozoic, middle life, was the age of reptiles. The Cenozoic, recent life, is the age of mammals and flowering plants.

slides.heading: Quick check: half-life
slides.body_md: What is the half-life of carbon-14?
slides.narration: Quick check. It is a little under six thousand years.

slides.heading: Quick check: connecting link
slides.body_md: Archaeopteryx links which two groups?

slides.heading: Biogeographical evidence
slides.body_md: The **distribution** of organisms reflects their history. Islands such as the **Galapagos** have **endemic** species found nowhere else. **Australia**, isolated early, has many **marsupials**, which radiated to fill niches that **placental mammals** fill on other continents.

slides.narration: Marsupials in Australia look remarkably like placental mammals elsewhere, because they adapted to similar ways of life. This is convergent evolution between the two groups, while within Australia the marsupials diverged from one ancestor.

slides.heading: Adaptive radiation: Darwin’s finches

On the **Galapagos Islands**, **Charles Darwin** saw finches with beaks suited to **seeds, insects, cactus flowers, grubs and buds**, all descended from a **seed-eating ancestor**.

slides.heading: Molecular evidence
slides.body_md: All living organisms share the same basic chemistry: **DNA** as genetic material, the **nearly universal genetic code**, **ATP** as energy currency, and similar proteins. The **more closely related** two species are, the **more similar** their DNA and proteins.

slides.narration: If all life shares one genetic code and the same energy molecule, it most likely descended from a common ancestor. Differences in DNA and proteins build up with time, so they act as a molecular record of how closely species are related.

Eras: Precambrian, Palaeozoic (fishes, amphibians, ferns), Mesozoic (reptiles, gymnosperms), Cenozoic (mammals, flowering plants).

notes.title: Evolution: Origin of Life and Evidences — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Theories of the origin of life
sections.body_md:
**Abiogenesis (spontaneous generation):** living organisms arise from non-living matter (for example, maggots from rotting meat). **Louis Pasteur** disproved it for present-day conditions with **swan-neck flasks**: boiled broth in a flask with a curved neck stayed sterile because dust and microbes were trapped in the bend; when the neck was broken, microbes grew.

**Biogenesis:** life arises only from pre-existing life — true of life today.

**Panspermia (cosmozoic theory):** spores or other units of life reached Earth from outer space (supported by early thinkers such as Arrhenius). It does not explain how life began in the first place.

**Oparin–Haldane theory (chemical evolution).** **A. I. Oparin (1924)** and **J. B. S. Haldane (1929)** proposed that the first life arose from non-living organic molecules by a long series of chemical reactions. The early atmosphere was **reducing**: **methane (CH₄), ammonia (NH₃), hydrogen (H₂) and water vapour**, with **no free oxygen**. Energy from **lightning, UV radiation (no ozone layer)** and **volcanic heat** formed simple organic molecules — sugars, amino acids, nitrogen bases, fatty acids — which collected in the oceans as a **“hot dilute soup”** (Haldane). These combined into larger molecules (proteins, nucleic acids).

**Why a reducing atmosphere was essential:** free oxygen is highly reactive and would **oxidise and break down** organic molecules as soon as they formed; without it, organic molecules could **accumulate**. The lack of ozone also let **UV radiation** reach the surface as an energy source.

**Protobionts** are aggregates of abiotically produced molecules surrounded by a membrane-like boundary, maintaining an internal environment different from the surroundings. They are not living but show some properties of cells (growth, simple division, selective uptake). Two kinds: **coacervates** (Oparin) — colloidal droplets of proteins, polysaccharides and water that absorb substances from the surroundings; and **microspheres** (Sidney Fox) — protein-like droplets formed when amino acids are heated and then cooled in water. The first true cells (heterotrophic, anaerobic prokaryotes) probably arose about 3.5 billion years ago.

Origin of life only from pre-existing life.
Idea that life reached Earth from outer space.
Abiotic aggregate of organic molecules with a boundary; a precursor of cells.

rows: Life from organic molecules in a reducing atmosphere

sections.heading: 2. The Miller–Urey experiment
sections.body_md:
In **1953**, **Stanley Miller**, working with **Harold Urey**, tested the Oparin–Haldane idea. A closed glass apparatus contained **methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour**. Water was **boiled** in one flask to send vapour round the system; in a larger flask, **electrodes** produced **electric sparks** (representing lightning); a **condenser** cooled the gases (representing rain), and the liquid collected in a **U-shaped trap**. After about **one week**, the liquid contained **amino acids** such as **glycine, alanine and aspartic acid**. Later similar experiments produced sugars, nitrogen bases, pigments and fats.

**Conclusion:** the organic molecules of life can be formed **abiotically** from simple inorganic gases when energy is supplied in a **reducing** atmosphere, supporting **chemical evolution**.

sections.heading: 3. Morphological evidence
sections.body_md:
**Homologous organs** have the **same basic structure and embryonic origin** but may perform **different functions**. Examples: **forelimbs** of human (grasping), cheetah (running), whale (swimming) and bat (flying), all with humerus, radius and ulna, carpals, metacarpals and phalanges; the **heart and brain** of vertebrates; in plants, the **thorn of Bougainvillea** and the **tendril of Cucurbita** (both modified stems). Homology shows **divergent evolution**: related organisms adapting to different needs.

**Analogous organs** perform the **same function** but differ in **structure and origin**. Examples: **wings of a butterfly and a bird**; **eye of an octopus and of a mammal**; **flippers of a penguin and a dolphin**; **sweet potato (modified root) and potato (modified stem)**. Analogy shows **convergent evolution**: unrelated organisms adapting to similar needs.

**Vestigial organs** are reduced and functionless (or nearly so) in an organism but functional in its ancestors or relatives. In humans: **vermiform appendix**, **nictitating membrane (plica semilunaris)**, **coccyx**, **muscles of the ear pinna**, **wisdom teeth**, body hair. They indicate **common descent**.

Same function, different origin; convergent evolution.
Reduced remnants of organs functional in ancestors.

sections.heading: 4. Embryological and palaeontological evidence
sections.body_md:
**Embryology.** Embryos of all vertebrates are alike in early stages, with **gill slits (pharyngeal pouches)**, a **notochord** and a **post-anal tail**. **Ernst Haeckel** proposed the **recapitulation theory (biogenetic law)**: “**ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny**” — the development of an individual repeats the evolutionary history of its group. **Karl Ernst von Baer** showed that embryos resemble the **embryos**, not the **adults**, of other animals, so the theory is not accepted literally; embryonic similarity is still evidence of **common ancestry**.

**Palaeontology.** **Fossils** are remains or impressions of past organisms preserved in **sedimentary rocks**. Deeper strata are older and contain simpler forms; younger strata contain more complex forms. **Connecting links** show features of two groups: **Archaeopteryx** (feathers and wings like birds; teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail like reptiles) links **reptiles and birds**.

**Dating fossils.** In living organisms the ratio of radioactive **carbon-14** to carbon-12 stays constant; after death, carbon-14 decays with a **half-life of 5730 years** and is not replaced. Age = number of half-lives × 5730 years (for example, one quarter left → 2 half-lives → **11460 years**). Radiocarbon dating is useful up to about **50 000 years**; older rocks are dated by **uranium–lead** or **potassium–argon** methods.

**Geological time scale** (approximate, million years ago):
- **Precambrian (before 541):** bacteria, algae, soft-bodied invertebrates.
- **Palaeozoic (541–252):** invertebrates (Cambrian), fishes (Devonian, “age of fishes”), amphibians (Carboniferous); pteridophytes and seed ferns form coal forests.
- **Mesozoic (252–66):** “age of reptiles” (dinosaurs); gymnosperms dominant; first mammals and birds (Jurassic); first flowering plants (Cretaceous).
- **Cenozoic (66–present):** “age of mammals”; angiosperms dominant; humans evolve in the Quaternary.

key_terms.definition_md: Organism with features of two groups, such as Archaeopteryx.
Time for half the radioactive atoms to decay; carbon-14: 5730 years.

sections.heading: 5. Biogeographical and molecular evidence; adaptive radiation
sections.body_md:
**Biogeography.** The distribution of species reflects their history. Oceanic islands (such as the **Galapagos**) have **endemic** species, related to but different from mainland species. **Australia**, separated early, has many **marsupials** and few native placental mammals.

**Adaptive radiation** is the evolution of different forms from one ancestral form, radiating into different habitats or niches. Examples:
- **Darwin’s finches** (Galapagos): from a **seed-eating ancestor**, finches evolved with beaks for **seeds, insects, cactus flowers, grubs in bark** and **buds and fruits**.
- **Australian marsupials**: from one ancestral stock, marsupial wolf, mole, sugar glider, numbat, kangaroo, koala and others evolved. Many resemble **placental mammals** on other continents (Tasmanian wolf and wolf; marsupial mole and mole; sugar glider and flying squirrel) — **convergent evolution** between the two groups.

**Molecular evidence.** All organisms use **DNA** (or RNA) as genetic material, a **nearly universal genetic code**, **ATP** as energy currency and similar enzymes and pathways. The degree of similarity in **DNA sequences** and **proteins** (for example **cytochrome c**, haemoglobin) reflects relatedness: human and chimpanzee DNA are about **98–99 percent** similar.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying Pasteur proved life arose from non-living matter (he disproved spontaneous generation).
- Including oxygen in the early atmosphere (it was reducing; free oxygen came later from photosynthesis).
- Calling coacervates living cells (they are non-living protobionts).
- Calling the wings of a bird and a bat analogous (as forelimbs they are homologous; as wings they are analogous — state which).
- Dating a dinosaur with carbon-14 (it is far too old; use uranium–lead).
- Writing that a quarter left means four half-lives (it means two).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a scientist, a gas, an example of an organ pair, a connecting link, a half-life.
- 2–3-mark questions: reducing atmosphere; protobionts vs coacervates; homologous vs analogous with examples; radiocarbon dating; adaptive radiation.
- 5-mark questions in parts: Miller–Urey with a labelled diagram; evidences of evolution; fossils and the geological time scale.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about Oparin’s coacervates is correct?

options.text_md: They are the first living bacteria.
They are protein droplets made by heating amino acids, as shown by Fox.
They are spores that reached Earth from space.

questions.solution_md: Coacervates are non-living protobionts of colloids; microspheres were Fox’s — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In Pasteur’s experiment, boiled broth in a swan-neck flask stayed free of microbes until the curved neck was broken off. What does this show?

options.text_md: Microbes in the broth came from microbes in the air, not from the broth itself.
Boiling creates microbes from broth.
Air alone turns broth into microbes.
Life arose by chemical evolution in the flask.

questions.solution_md: Once dust-borne microbes could reach the broth, it decayed: life comes from pre-existing life (biogenesis) — option (a).

options.text_md: abiogenesis
biogenesis
chemical evolution
panspermia

questions.solution_md: Panspermia, the cosmozoic theory — option (d).

options.text_md: primordial ozone layer
hot dilute soup
coacervate
swan-neck flask

questions.solution_md: Haldane’s “hot dilute soup” — option (b).

questions.stem_md: If the early Earth’s atmosphere had held as much free oxygen as it does today, what would most likely have happened to the first abiotically formed organic molecules?

options.text_md: They would have formed living cells more quickly.
They would have been protected from UV radiation and lasted longer.
They would have been oxidised and broken down before they could accumulate.
They would have turned into coacervates at once.

questions.solution_md: Free oxygen is highly reactive; a reducing atmosphere let organic molecules build up — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The first cells are thought to have been anaerobic heterotrophs. Which pair of early-Earth conditions explains this?

options.text_md: There was plenty of oxygen, and light was scarce.
There was an ozone layer, and no organic molecules.
There were many plants to eat, and no water.
There was no free oxygen, and organic molecules were plentiful in the oceans.

questions.solution_md: Without oxygen they had to be anaerobic; the “soup” supplied ready-made food — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Organic molecules formed abiotically could accumulate in the early oceans.

**Reason (R):** The early atmosphere had no free oxygen to oxidise them.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the absence of free oxygen explains why the molecules survived to accumulate — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Protein-like droplets formed by heating amino acids and then cooling them in water were named ______ by Sidney Fox.
questions.solution_md: Microspheres.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: ultraviolet radiation was an important energy source for chemical evolution on the early Earth.

answer.model_answer_md: There was **no ozone layer**, so strong **UV radiation reached the surface** and supplied energy for reactions.

questions.solution_md: No ozone layer.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between abiogenesis and biogenesis, and state which one describes the origin of living things today.

answer.model_answer_md: **Abiogenesis** (spontaneous generation) states that living things arise from **non-living matter**. **Biogenesis** states that life arises only from **pre-existing life**. Since Pasteur’s swan-neck flask experiment, **biogenesis** is accepted for living things **today**.

questions.solution_md: Two definitions; biogenesis today.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between protobionts and coacervates.

answer.model_answer_md: **Protobionts** is the general term for **non-living aggregates** of abiotically made organic molecules with a **membrane-like boundary** that keep an internal environment. **Coacervates** are **one kind** of protobiont, proposed by **Oparin**: **colloidal droplets** of **proteins and polysaccharides** in water.

questions.solution_md: General term vs a particular kind.

marking_scheme.step: Coacervates as one kind, Oparin, colloids

questions.stem_md: A student claims that the first organic molecules could form just as easily under today’s conditions. Using the Oparin–Haldane theory, give three reasons why this is unlikely.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Today’s air has **free oxygen**, which would **oxidise and destroy** organic molecules as they formed; the early atmosphere was **reducing**. (ii) The **ozone layer** now **blocks most UV radiation**, removing a major **energy source** for abiotic synthesis. (iii) Any organic molecules formed today would quickly be **eaten by existing microbes**, so they could not **accumulate** into a “soup”.

questions.solution_md: Oxygen, ozone, microbes.

questions.stem_md: Explain the Oparin–Haldane theory of the origin of life.

answer.model_answer_md: **Oparin (1924)** and **Haldane (1929)** proposed **chemical evolution**. The early atmosphere was **reducing** — **methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour**, **no free oxygen**. Energy from **lightning, UV radiation and volcanic heat** formed **simple organic molecules** (sugars, amino acids, bases), which collected in the oceans as a **“hot dilute soup”**. These joined into **larger molecules**, which aggregated as **protobionts** such as **coacervates**, from which the **first cells** arose.

questions.solution_md: Chemical evolution in steps.

marking_scheme.step: Energy forms organic molecules in a soup

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name and explain three theories of the origin of life other than chemical evolution. [2]
(b) Distinguish between Oparin’s coacervates and Fox’s microspheres. [2]
(c) Why can life not arise by chemical evolution on Earth today? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Abiogenesis** — life from non-living matter (disproved for today by **Pasteur**); **biogenesis** — life only from pre-existing life; **panspermia** — spores of life came from **outer space**.

(b) **Coacervates** (Oparin) are **colloidal droplets** of **proteins and polysaccharides** in water that can absorb substances and divide. **Microspheres** (Sidney Fox) are **protein-like droplets** formed by **heating amino acids** and cooling them in water. Both are **non-living protobionts**.

(c) Today’s atmosphere has **free oxygen** and an **ozone layer**, and existing **microbes** would consume any organic molecules, so they cannot **accumulate**.

questions.solution_md: Theories; protobionts; today.

questions.stem_md: Describe the Miller–Urey experiment and state its conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md: In **1953**, **Miller and Urey** sealed **methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour** in a glass apparatus. Water was **boiled** to circulate vapour; **electrodes** passed **sparks** through the gases (lightning); a **condenser** cooled them, and the liquid collected in a **trap**. After about a **week**, the liquid contained **amino acids** such as **glycine and alanine**. **Conclusion:** organic molecules can form **abiotically** from simple gases with energy in a **reducing** atmosphere, supporting **chemical evolution**.

questions.solution_md: Set-up, result, conclusion.

children.stem_md: Which bone group forms the largest part of the whale’s flipper in the figure?

options.text_md: Phalanges
Humerus
Carpals
Radius and ulna

children.solution_md: The whale’s phalanges are elongated to support the flipper — option (a).

children.stem_md: Compared with the four forelimbs, the wings of the housefly and the sparrow are

options.text_md: homologous, showing divergent evolution
analogous, showing convergent evolution
vestigial, showing loss of function
homologous, showing convergent evolution

children.solution_md: Same function, different origin (cuticle vs forelimb) — option (b).

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Explain why the four forelimbs are better evidence of common ancestry than the two kinds of wing.

answer.model_answer_md: The forelimbs share the **same bones in the same order** despite **different uses**, which is best explained by **inheritance from a common ancestor**. The wings share only **function**; similar needs can produce similar shapes in **unrelated** groups, so they do **not** show close common ancestry.

marking_scheme.step: Same plan despite different uses implies ancestry

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Name one homologous pair of organs in plants and explain why the pair is homologous.

answer.model_answer_md: The **thorn of Bougainvillea** and the **tendril of Cucurbita** are homologous: both arise from **axillary buds** as **modified stems**, though one gives **protection** and the other **support for climbing**.
